title: Chia Pudding
subtitle: Chia seeds soaked overnight in coconut milk, set like a gentle pudding
excerpt: Chia pudding is almost entirely hands-off: stir, refrigerate, sleep, eat. The seeds absorb the liquid overnight and swell into something thick and spoonable, with a gentle coconut sweetness and a texture that sits somewhere between rice pudding and thick yoghurt. The stirring step ten minutes in is not optional, skip it and the seeds clump into one solid mass at the bottom.
sourceNotes: Chia seeds as a food source originate with the Aztecs and Maya, who used them extensively as a staple crop. The modern chia pudding format emerged in Western health food culture in the 2010s, built on the seed's notable ability to absorb many times its weight in liquid.

recipe.batchNotes: Make up to 4 portions in individual jars. Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days. Top with fruit on the morning of eating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prepare the evening before. Stir after 10 minutes, then refrigerate overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: When chia seeds absorb liquid, they swell and release mucilage, a natural gelling agent, forming a thick, pudding-like texture around each seed. This is the same mechanism that sets the pudding overnight.

content.text: Chia pudding is built on a single property of chia seeds: they

when they meet liquid, swelling to many times their original size as they absorb it. Left overnight in coconut milk, they form a pudding that holds its shape in a spoon. The {{coconut-milk}} coconut milk from a tin gives it a rich creaminess that thinner plant milks can't match, the fat content is what makes it feel indulgent rather than watery. The critical step, and the one most people skip on the first attempt, is stirring again after the first ten minutes. At that point the seeds have begun to swell but haven't set, a quick stir redistributes any that have sunk into a clump before they solidify that way.

items.prepNote: for topping, or use any fresh fruit

content.text: Pour the {{coconut-milk}} coconut milk into a bowl or divide it between two jars. Shake the tin first, the cream and liquid separate in storage and both need to go in. Add the {{maple-syrup}} maple syrup and {{vanilla-extract}} vanilla extract and stir to combine. Tip in the {{chia-seeds}} chia seeds and whisk vigorously for a minute. The seeds are very light and tend to float rather than disperse, keep whisking until they're distributed throughout the liquid.
Leave the bowl uncovered for 10 minutes. Come back and stir again, this is the step that prevents clumping. By now the seeds will have started to swell slightly; stirring at this point ensures they
evenly throughout the liquid rather than bunching at the base. Cover and refrigerate overnight, or for a minimum of 6 hours.

In the morning, the pudding will be set and very thick. Give it a stir, if it's stiffer than you'd like, add a splash of plant milk to loosen it. Top with {{blueberries}} blueberries or whatever fresh fruit you have to hand. Eat cold.
Layer in a glass: chia pudding, then mango pieces, then another spoonful of pudding, it looks far more elaborate than it is.
Stir a teaspoon of cacao powder into the base before refrigerating. It sets as a chocolate pudding and tastes like a healthy dessert.
Swap coconut milk for almond milk for a lighter, less creamy pudding, reduce the chia seeds to 4 tbsp as almond milk is thinner and the ratio shifts.
A scattering of granola on top just before eating adds crunch against the soft pudding.
Seeds clumped at the bottom: the 10-minute stir was skipped. The pudding is still edible but has an uneven texture. Always stir once more partway through setting.
Pudding hasn't set after 8 hours: the chia seeds may be old. Seeds past their best lose some of their gelling ability. Check the date on the packet.
Too thick: add a tablespoon or two of plant milk in the morning and stir well to loosen.
